intro: Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 1 in D major, Op. 25, the “Classical”, lasts less than a quarter of an hour and has four movements, an Allegro, a Larghetto, a Gavotte and a Molto vivace finale. Nicolai Malko conducts the Philharmonia Orchestra.

cues.title: First movement, second subject
cues.text: The Allegro is a short movement in sonata form. Its fast first theme is followed by a second, in which staccato bassoons accompany the first violins. Prokofiev wrote for an orchestra of the size Haydn used, and the harmony departs from Haydn’s practice.
cues.evidence: Andrew Mellor, Philharmonia programme, 10 April 2025, p. 4, describes the first movement and its bassoon accompaniment. Gerard McBurney’s Boosey & Hawkes note gives the classical-sized instrumentation. https://philharmonia-assets.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/uploads/2025/04/03122720/10.04.25_RFH_online.pdf; https://www.boosey.com/cr/music/Serge-Prokofieff-Classical-Symphony-in-D-Symphony-No-1/4801
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition without a piano, 1917
cues.text: In the summer of 1917 Prokofiev left his piano behind and worked in the country near Petrograd. He composed much of the symphony without a keyboard, during long walks.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev’s autobiography, quoted by Herbert Glass in the Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note: summer 1917, the country near Petrograd, composing without a piano and during long walks. https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical

cues.title: Larghetto
cues.text: The Larghetto extends a single melody at length, where the Allegro moved quickly from one idea to the next. In this performance the two movements each last about four minutes.
cues.evidence: The four-movement order is printed on RCA Victor LM-2092; Herbert Glass describes the songful Larghetto. The two movements occupy approximately four minutes each in this transfer. https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical; https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-7-classical-symphony_sergei-prokofiev-nicolai-malko-philharmoni
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition and première, 1917–1918
cues.text: Prokofiev imagined Haydn alive in Prokofiev’s own century, keeping his style while admitting new elements. The symphony was completed in September 1917. Prokofiev conducted its première in Petrograd on 21 April 1918, after the October Revolution.
cues.evidence: Andrew Mellor, Philharmonia programme, 10 April 2025, p. 4: completion on 10 September 1917, première on 21 April 1918, and Prokofiev’s autobiographical account of Haydn. Herbert Glass identifies the composer as conductor. https://philharmonia-assets.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/uploads/2025/04/03122720/10.04.25_RFH_online.pdf; https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical

cues.title: Gavotte, third movement
cues.text: A gavotte stands where a minuet would normally come. Its dance steps are set over a succession of unexpected chords. Prokofiev also played the movement on the piano as a recital encore.
cues.evidence: Herbert Glass describes the Gavotte’s harmonic surprises; Andrew Mellor identifies the eighteenth-century dance and Prokofiev’s use of it as a piano encore. https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical; https://philharmonia-assets.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/uploads/2025/04/03122720/10.04.25_RFH_online.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Finale, Molto vivace
cues.text: The finale is marked Molto vivace. Prokofiev threw away his original finale and wrote this one afresh, setting himself the task of avoiding minor chords.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev’s autobiography, quoted by Herbert Glass, describes replacing the original finale and trying to avoid minor chords. The movement marking is Molto vivace. https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-1-classical
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Original LP coupling with Seventh Symphony
cues.text: The original LP placed this first symphony beside Prokofiev’s Seventh, his last, completed in 1952. The Philharmonia Orchestra and Nicolai Malko played both. The First Symphony lasts fourteen minutes.
cues.evidence: RCA Victor LM-2092 sleeve and Irvine Kolodin’s notes identify both symphonies, performers and the Seventh’s completion in 1952. https://archive.org/download/lp_symphony-no-7-classical-symphony_sergei-prokofiev-nicolai-malko-philharmoni/lp_symphony-no-7-classical-symphony_sergei-prokofiev-nicolai-malko-philharmoni_djvu.txt

composer.born: 27 April (15 April Old Style) 1891; Prokofiev himself gave 23 April, Sontsovka, Ukraine, then Russian Empire
composer.epithet: Twentieth-century composer known for Romeo and Juliet, with its writing for strings, and for his piano music.
facts: Glière at Sontsovka, 1902–03; St Petersburg Conservatory, 1904–14
Russia · United States · Bavaria · Paris; settled in Moscow in 1936
The Love for Three Oranges · Romeo and Juliet · Cinderella · War and Peace
Seven symphonies, five piano concertos and nine completed piano sonatas

quote.text: It seemed to me that if Haydn had lived into our own time, he would have kept his way of writing while taking in something new.
quote.source: Prokofiev, short Autobiography (1941), recalling the summer of 1917; our translation

composer.background:
At Sontsovka, the Ukrainian estate his father managed, Prokofiev grew up hearing his mother play Beethoven and Chopin. She wrote down his first piano pieces; the earliest, an Indian Galop, dates from 1896. After a trip to the Moscow opera in 1900, the eight-year-old set about writing an opera of his own, The Giant, for the family to perform at home. His mother eventually stopped playing when she saw that he had overtaken her. Sergei Taneyev recommended proper lessons, and Reinhold Glière spent the summers of 1902 and 1903 at Sontsovka teaching the boy, who was already filling manuscript books.

He entered the St Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen, bringing four operas, two sonatas, a symphony and piano pieces to the entrance examination. Rimsky-Korsakov taught orchestration, Lyadov harmony and counterpoint; later Anna Esipova took charge of his piano playing. Nikolai Tcherepnin taught conducting and encouraged his taste for Haydn and Mozart. His fellow student Nikolai Myaskovsky became the friend to whom he sent scores and complaints for the rest of his life. In December 1908 Prokofiev played some of his first distinctive pieces, Suggestion diabolique among them, at St Petersburg’s Evenings of Contemporary Music. The following spring his examination pieces shocked Lyadov, who heard Scriabin in them. In the final piano competition of 1914, with Esipova ill, Prokofiev played his own First Concerto. Glazunov opposed him, but Prokofiev was awarded the Rubinstein Prize, which was a grand piano.
